ambiguities.proposed_answer: It is the email. Sign-up takes {email, password}; POST /api/v1/sessions, SignInRequest and SignInResponse are unchanged; uniqueness is over the lower-cased email. A separate username changes the shape of the work: a new customers column, a new sign-in identifier, a change to a frozen request schema, and a decision about which of the two is the login key for the seeded accounts (AC16). If a distinct username is really wanted, this needs answering before design, not after.
ambiguities.question: Is the 'account name' at sign-up the existing email address, or a new separate username that is distinct from the email used to sign in?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: Accept the disclosure as inherent to AC6 and add one value to the catalogue: 409 account_unavailable, 'That account name is not available.', documented in openapi.yaml and blunted by the IP-keyed sign-up limit (A14). This grows a frozen contract artifact and knowingly trades away one enumeration property, so it is the architect's or requester's call rather than the implementer's. Fallback if the catalogue must not grow: 400 invalid_request with fields {email: 'unavailable'} — same disclosure, no new code, but a semantically wrong status.
ambiguities.question: How should a duplicate sign-up be refused on the wire, given the error catalogue is closed and no existing code fits, and given that any visible refusal makes sign-up an account-existence oracle in a service that goes to deliberate lengths elsewhere (identical 401s, timing-equalised sign-in, no 403/410) to avoid being one?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: 30 days, as a new app.links.anonymous-ttl defaulting to P30D. The codebase already reads 'about a month' as exactly 30 days for owner links, and a separate property means the anonymous figure can be tuned down for abuse reasons without changing what customers get.
ambiguities.question: Does 'expires one month after it is created' mean 30 days (matching the existing app.links.default-ttl of P30D) or a calendar month (P1M, so a link made on 31 January expires 28 February)?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: Client IP via request.getRemoteAddr(), the same key the CLICK, NOT_FOUND and SIGN_IN buckets already use, as a new ANONYMOUS_CREATE bucket with app.rate-limit.anonymous-create-per-minute defaulting to 10 — an order of magnitude under write-per-minute, so the anonymous path is never the cheaper way to create links.
ambiguities.question: Which key should the existing rate limiter use for an anonymous creator, and at what default, since there is no customer id?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: No. Keep getRemoteAddr, unchanged from today. Trusting a client-supplied header without a configured trusted-proxy list makes every IP-keyed limit spoofable, which is worse than the alternative. Record in the runbook that behind a load balancer every anonymous caller shares one bucket unless the proxy is configured to preserve the source address, and that this makes the default of 10/min a global figure rather than a per-caller one.
ambiguities.question: Should the IP-keyed buckets start trusting X-Forwarded-For now that an unauthenticated write endpoint depends on the IP key for its whole defence?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: POST /api/v1/customers for sign-up (a resource in the noun style the API already uses) and POST /api/v1/public/links for anonymous creation (the /public/ segment makes the unauthenticated surface visible in the route table and in the filter exemption, which is where a reviewer looks for it).
ambiguities.question: What should the two new endpoints be called?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: Only the account: 201 with {customerId, email, createdAt} and a Location of /api/v1/customers/{id}. AC5 describes signing in as a separate subsequent step, and issuing a token from an endpoint that is not the session endpoint duplicates the issuing path for no stated benefit.
ambiguities.question: Does sign-up return a session token, or only the created account?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: Minimum 12 characters, maximum 256 (matching SignInRequest), no composition rules, no denylist; a violation is 400 invalid_request with fields.password. The requirement speaks only to how passwords are held, so this is the smallest defensible rule that stops a one-character password.
ambiguities.question: What password rules apply at sign-up — minimum length, maximum, character classes?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: 201 with {code, shortUrl, longUrl, createdAt, expiresAt} and no Location. Location: /api/v1/links/{code} would point at a resource that answers 401 or 404 for every caller including the creator, which is a misleading contract. status and clickCount are omitted because AC13 says nobody may read an anonymous link's numbers, and a body shape that includes them invites a client to expect to fetch them later.
ambiguities.question: What does anonymous creation return, and does it carry a Location header?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: No. Scope is textual and numeric equivalent forms of what is written. The current code documents why DNS is off the create path — a name resolving publicly at create time can resolve internally at click time, and a lookup adds a dependency to a write path AC15/AC20 want kept thin. Adding resolution would be a new, separately-reviewable decision about SSRF, not part of closing these bypasses.
ambiguities.question: Does 'resist equivalent-form evasion generally' extend to resolving DNS at create time, so that a hostname pointing at 127.0.0.1 or an RFC1918 address is refused?

ambiguities.proposed_answer: Yes, expect the run to go to approval on the migration. With ddl-auto: validate there is no other way to make these changes, and both are one-way in production terms (relaxing a NOT NULL, and adding a constraint that can fail if case-variant emails already exist), so a human on the diff is the right routing rather than something to design around.
ambiguities.question: The schema changes this needs (customer_id nullable on links, a lower(email) unique constraint on customers) land in the Flyway migration directory, which the pipeline treats as protected. Is a human approval on those migrations expected as part of this run?

assumptions.rationale: AC1/AC2 are named as examples of a weak check, not the list. Today UrlValidator.isIpLiteral only matches dotted-quad or IPv6, so 2130706433 is never handed to InetAddress; and DenylistThreatCheck walks parents of the raw host, so 'malware.example.com.' never equals the seeded row. One normalisation point shared by both checks is what makes 'resists equivalent-form evasion generally' something a reviewer can verify.
assumptions.statement: Host normalisation is added at one point, applied before both the internal-host check and the denylist lookup, and covers: lower-casing, stripping trailing dot(s), IDN ToASCII/punycode, and parsing every numeric IPv4 form (decimal 2130706433, octal 0177.0.0.1, hex 0x7f.0.0.1, short forms 127.1) plus IPv4-mapped/compatible IPv6.

assumptions.rationale: RedirectController deliberately sets Location verbatim rather than via location(URI) 'so what was submitted is what is sent back'. Rewriting targets would change documented behaviour (AC17) and could re-point a shared link.
assumptions.statement: Normalisation is used for checking only. The stored long_url and the Location header remain byte-identical to what was submitted.

assumptions.rationale: Fail closed on a security check. 400 would additionally tell a probing caller which forms parse, and AC1 explicitly requires the trailing-dot form to answer 422, i.e. it must be normalised rather than treated as a syntax error.
assumptions.statement: A host that cannot be normalised unambiguously is refused with 422 url_rejected, not accepted and not 400.

assumptions.rationale: ThreatCheck's own javadoc records that the 'existing link found to point at one stops redirecting' half is served by the takedown path, not a rescan. Adding a sweeper is new machinery nobody asked for.
assumptions.statement: Item 1 is create-time only: no background rescan or retroactive re-evaluation of links created before the fix.

assumptions.rationale: AC5 requires the new credentials to sign in through the existing endpoint, which is email-keyed and frozen in openapi.yaml. A separate username column would mean a new sign-in field and a contract change to a documented endpoint, which AC17 and the out-of-scope list both push against. See ambiguity Q1.
assumptions.statement: 'Account name' is the existing email field: sign-up posts {email, password}, and SignInRequest/SignInResponse and POST /api/v1/sessions are untouched.

assumptions.rationale: AC6's concurrency clause cannot be met by a read-then-write. LinkService.insertWithAlias already uses exactly this pattern for aliases. The existing ux_customers_email is case-sensitive while SignInService uses findByEmailIgnoreCase, so without a lower(email) constraint two case-variant sign-ups both insert and the next sign-in for either fails on a non-unique result.
assumptions.statement: Uniqueness is enforced by a database constraint over the lower-cased email, added by a Flyway migration, and the concurrent-duplicate case is decided by catching the constraint violation rather than by a pre-check.

assumptions.rationale: AC7 says the stored representation is produced by the same mechanism the seeded accounts use. Reusing the bean rather than restating parameters also keeps the seeded V2 hashes verifiable.
assumptions.statement: Sign-up hashes through the existing PasswordHasher bean at its existing parameters; the raw password is never logged, never returned, and appears in no response body.

assumptions.rationale: findOwnedBy and findByDomainAndCodeAndCustomerId are both equality-scoped on customer_id, and NULL matches neither, so AC8/AC13 hold by construction rather than by a filter someone must remember. A sentinel customer is an account row that could in principle be signed into and whose list would expose every anonymous link.
assumptions.statement: An anonymous link is a links row with customer_id NULL, via a Flyway migration relaxing the NOT NULL; not a sentinel 'anonymous' customer row.

assumptions.rationale: Matches the existing app.links.default-ttl reading of 'about a month' as exactly 30 days, keeps the new limit configurable in the existing style, and refuses a caller-chosen expiry on a link nobody owns and nobody can delete. See ambiguity Q3.
assumptions.statement: Anonymous expiry is a new configurable app.links.anonymous-ttl defaulting to P30D, applied at creation as an absolute instant; the anonymous endpoint does not accept a caller-supplied expiresAt.

assumptions.rationale: SessionAuthenticationFilter is registered for /api/v1/* with only /api/v1/sessions exempt, so an unauthenticated endpoint needs an explicit exemption. Making the existing create endpoint dual-mode would change a documented 401 behaviour, which AC17 forbids.
assumptions.statement: Anonymous creation is a new path, and POST /api/v1/links with no token keeps answering 401 unauthorized. The new path is added to the session filter's exemption list beside /api/v1/sessions.

assumptions.rationale: Aliases share one namespace with generated codes and are never reissued after a soft delete, so an unidentified caller choosing memorable aliases is permanent namespace squatting with no owner to revoke it.
assumptions.statement: The anonymous request body carries longUrl only; alias and expiresAt are unknown properties and answer 400, per the existing strict-body rule.

assumptions.rationale: AC11, AC12 and AC15 then hold because the behaviour is literally the same code, not a parallel implementation that can drift. It also keeps the click path untouched, which is the stated priority.
assumptions.statement: Anonymous creation reuses the existing create path end to end: same UrlValidator, same ThreatCheck, same 22-char CSPRNG code generator and (domain, code) uniqueness, same resolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing, same 503 when that invalidation or a needed dependency fails.

assumptions.rationale: Uses the existing anti-abuse system rather than a new one (explicitly out of scope), and gives AC14's 'cannot be used to bypass the limits on authenticated creation' a concrete meaning: the anonymous ceiling is strictly tighter than the authenticated one, and neither path can spend the other's tokens.
assumptions.statement: Anonymous creation is charged to a new IP-keyed bucket added to the existing RateLimitBucket enum and RateLimiter, with a property in the existing app.rate-limit.*-per-minute style defaulting well below write-per-minute; the WRITE bucket stays keyed by customer id and is unchanged.

assumptions.rationale: Sign-up is the other unauthenticated endpoint that writes to PostgreSQL, and the non-functional line about an unauthenticated DB write not becoming an unmetered storage-burn vector applies to the customers table as much as to links.
assumptions.statement: Sign-up is rate limited by the same mechanism, keyed by client IP, even though the requirement only asks for it on item 3.

assumptions.rationale: That endpoint answers 202 for any well-formed code precisely so it is not an existence oracle; carving out anonymous codes would reintroduce one, and an unowned link is exactly the link most in need of a takedown path.
assumptions.statement: POST /api/v1/links/{code}/abuse-reports continues to answer 202 for an anonymous code, and a report still blocks that link immediately.

assumptions.rationale: The contract constraint says openapi.yaml must continue to describe the service, and the two docs currently assert in several places that registration does not exist and that all creation is authenticated.
assumptions.statement: artifacts/openapi.yaml, docs/API.md and docs/RUNBOOK.md are updated in the same change: new paths, any new error code, the new TTL and rate-limit properties, and the removal of 'no registration endpoint' claims.

assumptions.rationale: The constraint requires the failure to be produced and visible before the fix and the tests retained. @Disabled or a deleted test would satisfy the letter of 'the suite passes' and none of the intent.
assumptions.statement: The AC3 tests land as their own commit ahead of the fix commit, with the failing run recorded in the run log, and remain as ordinary enabled tests afterwards.
